books.section: Unit 5: Toward the Civil War and Reconstruction (1844–1877)

primary_sources: Amnesty Act of May 22, 1872, ch. 193, 17 Stat. 142

stimulus.text:
“That all political disabilities imposed by the third section of the fourteenth article of amendments of the Constitution of the United States are hereby removed from all persons whomsoever, except Senators and Representatives of the thirty-sixth and thirty-seventh Congresses, officers in the judicial, military, and naval service of the United States, heads of departments, and foreign ministers of the United States.”

—Amnesty Act, May 22, 1872 (17 Stat. 142)
stimulus.source_note: Amnesty Act of May 22, 1872, ch. 193, 17 Stat. 142. Public domain (federal statute; text verified against the Statutes at Large as quoted by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit and Congress.gov).

source: original; stimulus as noted in stimulus.source_note
stem: The Amnesty Act named the “third section of the fourteenth article.” That section had originally

options.text: barred former Confederates from holding office.
given Black men the right to vote.

rationales.A: Section 3 of the Fourteenth Amendment barred anyone who had sworn to uphold the Constitution and then joined the rebellion from holding office. The Amnesty Act removed that bar for nearly all of them.
rationales.B: Background: voting rights are in the Fifteenth Amendment, not the Fourteenth.
rationales.C: Background: slavery was abolished by the Thirteenth Amendment.
rationales.D: Background: the military districts came from the Reconstruction Acts of 1867.
rationales.general:
1. The Act removes “political disabilities imposed by the third section.”
2. A disability is a penalty, and this one was the ban on holding office.
3. It fell on men who had sworn an oath to the Constitution and then joined the rebellion.
4. The Act lifts the ban, which only makes sense if the ban had kept them out of office.
Remember: to read a repeal, first ask what was being repealed.
